name: AI agent and crawler names
plain: AI crawlers and browsing agents often announce themselves by name in the User-Agent header.
meaning: Operators publish names such as GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-User, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended. Many split them into training crawlers, search crawlers and fetchers that run when a person asks a question. Sites can allow or block them in robots.txt (RFC 9309). A name is only a claim unless the operator also publishes IP ranges or signs requests.

web.api: User-Agent request header; robots.txt product tokens (RFC 9309)

steps: Agent sends a User-Agent with its product name
Site reads the header and robots.txt rules
Site allows, limits or blocks by name
Site may verify IP ranges or signatures

chrome.note: Not browser behavior; sent by agent and crawler operators

fields.name: User-Agent
fields.range: product token and URL of the operator

fields.name: robots.txt rule
fields.range: allow or disallow for a product token

limits.headline: Can tell which AI operator sent a request, if it tells the truth
can: Read the agent's name from the header
Apply robots.txt rules per product token
Separate training crawlers from user triggered fetchers
Check IP lists to confirm a claim
cannot: See the question the person asked
Cover agents that pose as a normal browser
limits.differs: Many browsing agents run a normal Chrome and send a normal user agent, so names catch only the declared ones.

story.what_it_is: AI services often introduce themselves by name. Sites decide whether to let each one in.

marketing.name: Overview of OpenAI crawlers
marketing.pitch: Docs list the user agents and what each one does.

story.for_you: You never see it. When you ask an AI to read a page, a fetcher may visit with its own name, which the site can allow or block.
story.for_makers: Decide per name and per purpose: training, search, user requested. Confirm claims with published IP ranges or signatures. Keep your list current because names and tokens change.

use_cases.example: A publisher blocks training crawlers but allows search crawlers.
A retailer allows user triggered fetchers so shoppers can compare prices through an assistant.
A firewall rule rate limits any client that claims an AI crawler name without matching IP ranges.
Traffic reports separate AI fetchers from human visits.
A docs site allows AI fetchers so developers get answers with citations.
A university site blocks training crawlers on course notes.

risks: Blocking may hide a site from AI search

technical_bounds: Claim only; verify by IP or signature
Agents using a normal browser look like people

history.change: Robots Exclusion Protocol published as RFC 9309
Google reported to list Google-Agent as a user triggered fetcher
